source.title: Singular Vectors of Attention Heads Align with Features
source.authors: Gabriel Franco; Carson Loughridge; Mark Crovella

record.file_problem: not stated; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests superposition-related feature geometry in an extended toy autoencoder with attention, a different setup from the original toy-model study. It also tests whether overlapping feature directions occur when feature pairs exceed head capacity.
record.gate_note: The toy-model alignment, orthogonalization, sparsity, anisotropy, and over-capacity results are reported. Real-model sparse attention decomposition is reported as a prediction consistent with alignment, but it does not directly establish feature identities or test the specific LLM evidence claims V4 and V5. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as results. GPT-2 SAE anisotropy values are used to set an experiment range, not treated as a result about SAE feature recovery.
record.test_reason: The paper is mainly about singular-vector–feature (SVF) alignment in attention heads, which is not a superposition claim. It does report its own toy-model geometry results bearing on V1. Without the head (N=20, D=10), features form antipodal pairs, reproducing the original. With the head, the features of interest orthogonalize while the rest stay superposed in the remaining subspace. Most other rows measure alignment, not superposition, so they bear on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. When features are linearly represented, attention-head singular vectors tend to align with features of interest. This is shown in a toy model and supported by theorems. Sparse attention decomposition is a testable prediction, observed in Pythia and GPT-2. Over-capacity, anisotropy and multi-head questions are left open.
record.recipe_differences: Builds on the toy autoencoder used in the original superposition work, adding an attention head trained on feature-pair attention targets and a joint attention/reconstruction objective; it also studies singular-vector alignment and over-capacity behavior.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment depends on whether feature pairs occur often enough for optimization: the paper reports robust alignment down to p = 0.038 and insufficient occurrences at p = 0.038 or less. Feature sharing also changes when feature-pair count exceeds head dimension. The study reports robustness sweeps over loss weight, feature count, head dimension, context length, and random seeds.

fits_no_version.finding: Attention-head singular vectors align with the feature pairs the head attends to, in order of target-logit importance. Alignment holds across λ, N, H, context length and seeds, and drops at p≤0.038 (r2, r4–r7, r10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy models, QK singular vectors align with features of interest to an attention head.

fits_no_version.finding: When feature pairs exceed head dimension, high-logit pairs get dedicated singular vectors while the lowest-logit features collapse onto the smallest singular vector and become indistinguishable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Capacity-limited attention heads superpose their least important features onto a shared direction (head-space analogue of capacity-based allocation).

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse attention decomposition emerges over training in Pythia-160M IOI heads and is present in GPT-2 IOI heads. It disappears under spectrum-preserving rotations of the SVD bases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Real-model attention decomposes sparsely in the SVD basis, consistent with SVF alignment.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: Real-model feature identities are not directly observed; the authors state that real-model alignment cannot be conclusively established without prior knowledge of feature representations. The over-capacity experiment is described as preliminary. Several key comparisons are presented in figures, and the paper reports that not all tested Pythia heads show strong sparsity emergence.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Parameter-sweep heatmap entries and individual Pythia head decompositions are not separately transcribed; the paper's aggregate robustness statements and its stated differing-head result are recorded instead.

untested.parts: Sparsity-dependent phase transition: the sparsity sweep measures alignment, not storage geometry. Geometry is shown only at default p=0.52 for N=20/D=10 (and N=100/D=50 with the head).
No neuron-level polysemanticity is measured. The head-capacity analogue is recorded under fits_no_version.
Real-model results are sparse attention decomposition in the SVD basis. GPT-2 SAE anisotropy is used only to set an experimental range.
Features are 1-D vectors by construction; there is no comparison with multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Feature geometry with 100 features in 50 dims and 20 pairs of interest: features of interest orthogonalize against the rest
Approximately isotropic WWᵀ with and without two features of interest

record.verdict_notes: The superposition content is limited to a warm-up replication of the original toy geometry (r1) and the reshaping of that geometry by an attention objective (r3). The rest of the paper uses the toy model as a tool for a different question. The GPT-2 SAE anisotropy (‖E_X‖ 10–55) describes SAE dictionary geometry and is not a test of V4/V5.

versions.untested_parts: The toy model tests feature alignment and geometry under selected sparsities and capacities; it does not establish the same geometry in real models or give a general transition law across all sparsity levels.
The study examines feature pairs and attention-head dimensions in toy models, not polysemantic neurons or neuron-level feature allocation.
The study does not investigate alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
The real-model results measure sparse decomposition of attention in an SVD basis, not features spread across neurons or sparse features recovered by an SAE.
The study does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.

The toy model represents features as vectors and finds alignment or sharing along singular-vector directions; it does not compare one-dimensional with multi-dimensional feature representations in real models.

rows.subject: toy model without attention head
rows.operation_detail: Measured cosine geometry of learned features in the toy autoencoder without an attention head.
rows.value: Features arrange into 10 pairs, one per dimension, with each pair antipodal; the arrangement is described as isotropic.
rows.note: The paper describes this arrangement as minimizing interference in reconstruction.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, Figure 1(a) and accompanying paragraph; Appendix C.1, Figure 19(a).

rows.subject: toy model (N = 20, D = 10, H = 10)
rows.stage_stated: trained for 10,000 steps in the example described
rows.operation_detail: Trained the feature autoencoder and an attention head on a target that attends when one specified feature is in the query and another is in the key.
rows.baseline: Toy model without the attention head is described as isotropic; no numeric baseline stated.
rows.value: w0 aligns with left singular vector u0 and w1 with right singular vector v0; the spectrum has one large singular value.
rows.note: The model's feature representations are vectors, and the reported alignment is with individual singular-vector directions.
rows.check: Measures SVF alignment, not how features are stored. Features are vectors by construction, so it cannot test V6 (1-D vs multi-D) or V1.

rows.subject: toy model (N = 20, D = 10, H = 10)
rows.operation_detail: Measured the geometry of learned features after adding an attention head for a feature pair of interest.
rows.measure: Orthogonality of features of interest to other features
rows.baseline: Without the attention head, the paper reports an isotropic arrangement; no numeric baseline stated.
rows.value: The two features of interest are orthogonal to all other features; remaining features shift into the subspace orthogonal to their span.
rows.note: The authors attribute this geometry to minimizing reconstruction interference.
rows.check: Keep linked to V1 only. It shows the toy model's superposition geometry reshaped by the attention objective: features of interest become orthogonal, the rest occupy the remaining D−2 dimensions (approximately isotropic per Fig. 19b).

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, Figure 1(b) and accompanying discussion; Appendix C.1, Figure 19(b).

rows.subject: toy model (N = 100, D = 50)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with target logits declining linearly across 20 feature pairs of interest, Ti,i+20 = 26 − i for 0 ≤ i < 20.
rows.value: The paper reports that all features align with singular vectors and that singular values reflect target-logit values.
rows.note: The text reports alignment across multiple feature pairs but does not provide numeric cosine values here.
rows.check: Alignment result, not a superposition-geometry measure; it does not bear on V1 or V6. The Fig. 1(c) orthogonalization geometry is a separate result not captured here.

rows.subject: toy model (N = 20, D = 10)
rows.operation_detail: Tracked feature and singular-vector cosines during training for four feature pairs of interest.
rows.measure: Alignment over training and order of alignment
rows.value: The highest-impact feature pairs align first; u0 moves into its final position around step 1500, and the next mode changes through about step 4000. The paper reports the pattern repeating for remaining pairs.
rows.note: Feature and singular-vector changes are described as evolving in tandem.
rows.check: Training dynamics of SVF alignment; not a measure of superposition.

rows.subject: toy model (default settings)
rows.operation_detail: Swept feature probability p and measured alignment of designated features with singular vectors.

conditions.value: swept from 1 down to 0.02 in exponentially declining steps
default settings; four feature pairs of interest

rows.value: The paper states that alignment occurs robustly down to p = 0.038; at p = 0.038 or less, feature pairs do not occur often enough in the input for the model to optimize for them.
rows.locator: Appendix A.2, Figures 12–13 and accompanying text
rows.note: The aggregate statement describes the sweep; individual heatmap entries are not transcribed as separate values.
rows.check: The sparsity sweep measures SVF alignment, not the sparsity-dependent superposition transition. Fig. 12 shows alignment ~1.00 for p≥0.074 but mixed values at p=0.038, so 'robust down to 0.038' is loose; the state for alignment is observed above 0.038.

rows.subject: toy model (default settings)
rows.operation_detail: Measured singular-vector/feature alignment at feature probability p = 0.02.
rows.value: The paper states that a given feature pair occurs in less than 1% of inputs at p = 0.02, and that feature pairs at this sparsity do not occur often enough for optimization.
rows.locator: Appendix A.2, Figure 12 and accompanying text
rows.note: Figure 12 displays individual alignment values, but the paper's text attributes the failure to insufficient feature-pair occurrences.
rows.check: Alignment failure at p=0.02, attributed to too-rare feature pairs; not a test of V1's sparsity transition.

rows.subject: toy model (N = 20, D = 10, H = 5)
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number of feature pairs of interest beyond the head dimension, with target logits declining by pair index.
rows.measure: Feature alignment with singular vectors and sharing of singular-vector directions
rows.baseline: Capacity case: 5 feature pairs for H = 5.
rows.value: Features with the lowest target logits are assigned to the smallest singular vector; the paper says most singular vectors still map to a single feature.
rows.locator: Appendix E, Figure 23(a) and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors say features mapped to the same singular vector cannot be distinguished and may be mistakenly associated across pairs.
rows.check: Measures allocation of feature pairs to head singular vectors (head-space capacity), not neuron polysemanticity (V2) or feature dimensionality (V6). Recorded under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: toy model (N = 40, D = 20, H = 10)
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number of feature pairs of interest beyond the head dimension, with target logits declining by pair index.
rows.measure: Feature alignment with singular vectors and sharing of singular-vector directions
rows.baseline: Capacity case: 10 feature pairs for H = 10.
rows.value: The paper reports that the effect persists at this higher capacity: lowest-logit features share the smallest singular vector, while most singular vectors still map to a single feature.
rows.locator: Appendix E, Figure 23(b) and accompanying text
rows.note: This is a preliminary study; the authors state that more work is needed to understand the general over-capacity regime.

rows.subject: toy model (N = 20, D = 10, H = 10)
rows.operation_detail: Froze the feature dictionary, varied its anisotropy, trained only the attention head, and measured feature-to-singular-vector alignment.
rows.measure: Mean cosine alignment; raw and anti-whitened alignment also plotted
rows.baseline: Isotropic features permit exact alignment by construction.
rows.value: For anisotropy close to the maximum seen in GPT-2, mean raw cosine similarity is above 0.75; anti-whitening can improve alignment.
rows.uncertainty: Mean ± one standard deviation across runs
rows.note: The text describes the plotted result but does not state the precise cosine value at each anisotropy level.
rows.check: Alignment under imposed anisotropy with a frozen dictionary; not a superposition measure.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M
rows.stage_stated: training checkpoints at intervals of 1000 training epochs; 130 checkpoints
rows.operation_detail: Measured the sparsity of relative-attention decompositions in the SVD basis for IOI circuit heads and token pairs across training.

conditions.value: heads and token pairs listed in Table 2; results averaged across those heads

rows.baseline: Start of training, compared with later checkpoints; no numeric baseline stated in text.
rows.value: The paper reports that sparsity emerges during training in a manner similar to the toy model; not all attention heads show strong sparsity emergence.
rows.note: This is evidence for the paper's sparse-attention-decomposition prediction, not direct measurement of feature identities or the specific LLM claims V4–V5.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Measured the minimum number of singular-vector terms needed to reconstruct relative attention for IOI prompts.

conditions.value: 128 prompts varying names, templates including name order, and objects
IOI attention heads shown in Figure 9(a)

rows.measure: Nrecon, number of singular vectors needed to reconstruct relative attention
rows.value: The paper reports that Nrecon is small in most cases, with typical values varying by attention-head role.
rows.note: This is an attention-decomposition result, not direct evidence of SAE-recovered features or feature distribution across neurons.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M
rows.operation_detail: Randomly rotated the left and right singular-vector bases while preserving the matrix spectrum and rank, then recomputed decomposition sparsity.
rows.value: The decline in S(v) disappears under random rotations; the paper concludes observed sparsity depends on the specific alignment of directions with singular vectors.
rows.note: This control rules against sparsity being explained merely by low rank or a few large singular values.

relationships.condition: Toy autoencoder N=20, D=10, p=0.52, with and without an attention head
relationships.reason: Without the head, features form 10 antipodal pairs, isotropically arranged (r1). With the head, non-interest features remain superposed in the orthogonal complement (r3).
relationships.display_finding: Without the head, features formed 10 isotropically arranged antipodal pairs. With the head, features not of interest stayed superposed in the orthogonal complement.

reader_labels.reason: The toy model shows feature/singular-vector alignment and feature orthogonalization; in multi-pair settings, aligned feature pairs are reported up to head capacity (r2–r6).

reader_labels.reason: At extreme sparsity, feature pairs occur too rarely for optimization; above head capacity, lower-logit features share a direction and cannot be distinguished (r7–r9).

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.reason: The reported features align with individual singular-vector directions in ordinary cases, and over-capacity sharing occurs on a singular-vector direction (r2, r4, r8–r9).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
